THE BRIEF REASONS FOR THE JUDGMENT:
1. Briefly stated the case of the prosecution is that on 21.4.2011 at about 11.15 pm at E Block, Sector 15. Rohini, Delhi within the jurisdiction of PS KNK Marg, the accused was driving a TATA Indica bearing No. DL 8CM 2612 on a public way in a rash or negligent manner so as to endanger human life and personal safety of others and he struck against one scooter no. DL 8SV 7749 as a result of which Sh. Tushar Ahuja received simple injuries and Sh. Puneet received grievous injuries.
He was chargesheeted for the offences punishable under Section 279/337/338 IPC.

I have heard the arguments of Ld. APP for State and Ld. Counsel for the accused.
I have also perused the record carefully.
16. In a criminal trial, the onus remains on the prosecution to prove the guilt of accused beyond all reasonable doubts and benefit of doubt, if any, must necessarily go in favour of the accused.
It is for the prosecution to travel the entire distance from may have to must have.
If the prosecution appears to be improbable or lacks credibility the benefit of doubt necessarily has to go to the accused.

In this regard, it is relevant to reproduce the observations made by Hon'ble Supreme Court in Kali Ram Vs.
Himanchal Pradesh (1973 2 SCC 808) in para 23 and 25 which are reproduced as under:
" 23.

Observations in a recent decision of this Court, Shivaji Sahabrao Bobade & Anr.
v. State of Maharashtra (1973 2 SCC 793) to which reference has been made during arguments were not intended to make a departure from the rule of the presumption of innocence of the accused and his entitlement to the benefit of reasonable doubt in criminal cases.

Shivaji Sahabrao Bobade & Anr.
v. State of Maharashtra (1973 2 SCC 793)
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: One of the cardinal principles which has always to be kept in view in our system of administration of justice for criminal cases is that a person arraigned as an accused is presumed to be innocent unless that presumption is rebutted by the prosecution by production of evidence as may show him to be guilty of the offence with which he is charged.
The burden of proving the guilt of the accused is upon the prosecution and unless it relieves itself of that burden, the courts cannot record a finding of the guilt of the accused.

There are certain cases in which statutory presumptions arise regarding the guilt of the accused, but the burden even in those cases is upon the prosecution to prove the existence of facts which have to be present before the presumption can be drawn.

Once those facts are shown by the prosecution to exist, the court can raise the statutory presumption and it would, in such an event,
be for the accused to rebut the presumption.
The onus even in such cases upon the accused is not as heavy as is normally upon the prosecution to prove the guilt of the accused.

If some material is brought on the record consistent with the innocence of the accused which may reasonably be true, even though it is not positively proved to be true, the accused would be entitled to acquittal.

Leaving aside the cases of statutory presumptions, the onus is upon the prosecution to prove the different ingredients of the offence and unless it discharges that onus, the prosecution cannot succeed...

25. Another golden thread which runs through the web of the administration of justice in criminal cases is that if two views are possible on the evidence adduced in the case, one pointing to the guilt of the accused and the other to his innocence, the view which is favourable to the accused should be adopted.
This principle has a special relevance in cases wherein the guilt of the accused is sought to be established by circumstantial evidence.

Rule has accordingly been laid down that unless the evidence adduced in the case is consistent only with the hypothesis of the guilt of the accused and is inconsistent with that of his innocence, the court should refrain from recording a finding of guilt of the accused.

It is also an accepted rule that in case the 73 5 court entertains reasonable doubt regarding the, guilt of the accused, the State vs . Mukul Singh on 9 March, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/12061482/
6 accused must have the benefit of that doubt.

Of course, the doubt regarding the guilt of the accused should be reasonable : it is not the doubt of a mind which is either so vacillating that it is incapable of reaching a firm conclusion or so timid that it is hesitant and afraid to take things to their natural consequences.
The rule regarding the benefit of doubt also does not warrant acquittal of the accused by resort to surmises, conjectures or fanciful considerations.

As mentioned by us recently in the case of State of Punjab v. Jagir Singh,(1974 2 SCC 227) a criminal trial is not like a fairy tale wherein one is free to give flight to one's imagination and fantasy.

sentences.text: It concerns itself with the question as to whether the accused arraigned at the trial is guilty of the offence with which he is charged.
Crime is an event in real life and is the product of interplay of different human emotions.

In arriving at the conclusion about the guilt of the accused charged with the commission of a crime, the, court has to judge, the evidence by the yardstick of probabilities, its intrinsic worth and the animus of witnesses.
Every case in the final analysis would have to depend upon its own facts.

Although the benefit of every reasonable doubt should be given to the accused, the courts should not at the same time reject evidence which is ex facie trustworthy, on grounds which are fanciful or in the nature of conjectures."
17. The case of the prosecution is that on 21.04.2011 at about 11:15 P.M, the Injured Puneet was riding his Scooter bearing registration No. DL 8SV 7749 along with pilion rider injured/Tushar Ahuja.

When they were in front of gate of EBlock, Sector 15, Rohini, the accused who was driving the offending vehicle bearing registration No. DL 8SCM 2612 TATA Indica car hit the scooter driven by the injured Puneet and Tushar from right side while turning his car to EBlock due to which injured Puneet received grievous injury and Tushar received simple injury.
The accused was charged with offences punishable u/s 279/337/338 IPC.

Section 279 IPC reads as under :
279. Rash driving or riding on a public way.--Whoever drives any vehicle, or rides, on any public way in a manner so rash or negligent as to endanger human life, or to be likely to cause hurt or injury to any other person, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to six months, or with fine which may extend to one thousand rupees, or with both.

Section 337 IPC reads as under :
337. Causing hurt by act endangering life or personal safety of others.

Whoever causes hurt to any person by doing any act so rashly or negligently as to endanger human life, or the personal safety of others, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to six months, or with fine which may extend to five hundred rupees, or with both.

Section 338 IPC reads as under :

Causing grievous hurt by act endangering life or personal safety of others Whoever causes grievous hurt to any person by doing any act so rashly or negligently as to endanger human life, or the personal safety of others, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine which may extend to one thousand rupees, or with both.

Therefore, in order to secure conviction against the accused persons, the prosecution is required to prove the following:
i.
That Sh. Puneet received grievous injury and Sh. Tushar Ahuja received simple injury.
ii. That the injuries received by the injured persons due to the accident caused by the offending vehicle which was driven by the accused.
iii. That the accident occurred on account of rashness or negligence on the part of accused in driving the vehicle.
18. The accused admitted the genuineness and preparation of MLC bearing No 3035/11 and 3034/11 along with Xray report and plate as well as the mechanical inspection report Ex. A1 (colly).

PW Dr.
Deepti Bhalla has deposed that the nature of injury suffered by Tushar Ahuja was grievous and that of Puneet was simple in nature.
PW Dr Deepti was not cross examined by the accused.
It is therefore, sufficiently proved that the injured Puneet received grievous injury and Tushar Ahuja received simple injury which was due to road accident.

19. Prosecution examined the Bajrang Singh, owner of the offending vehicle during the prosecution evidence who deposed that on 21.04.2011, the offending vehicle was in the possession of his son i.e.
the accused Mukul Singh.

He admitted that he was being served with notice u/s 133 M.V Act Ex.
PW2/A to which he replied with Ex. PW2/A.
The accused did not dispute the mechanical inspection report Ex. A19 (colly).
The offending vehicle was found to be having damage on the right side of the body while the scooter of the injured persons was also found to be having damage on right side of the body.
Therefore, this Court is of the considered opinion that there is no dispute regarding the identity of the accused as well as offending vehicle.

20. Now, the most essential ingredient to be proved by the prosecution for securing the conviction for the charge under section 279/337/338 IPC is that the injuries suffered by the injured persons is the direct result of the rash or negligent driving by the accused.
It is pertinent to mention that PW Raj Kumar stated in his testimony that the accused fled the spot after the accident.
Whereas PW Puneet stated that PW Raj Kumar apprehended the accused after the accident and that they were taken to BSA hospital in the offending vehicle of the accused.
Whereas PW Raj Kumar stated in his testimony that he along with Puneet took injured Tushar to Satyam hospital.
It is pertinent to mention that as per the MLC, injured Puneet received grievous injuries and thus, the statement of PW Raj Kumar cannot be accepted that he along with Puneet took Tushar to hospital.
PW Puneet also stated that they were taken to BSA hospital and then from BSA hospital to Satyam hospital.

This deposition is contrary to the deposition made by PW Raj Kumar and PW Dr. Deepti Bhalla.
It is also pertinent to mention that PW Dr. Deepti Bhalla stated that injured were brought by ASI Sarju Singh.
The prosecution did not examine ASI Sarju Singh.
It is admitted position in the case that the injured had first taken to Satyam Hospital where they were given primary medical care but the prosecution did not examine any witness in this regard.

It is pertinent to mention that PW Ct Ravinder stated in his testimony that the scooter of the injured/PW Puneet was seized from the spot of incident whereas PW SI Rajesh Kumar who was the first IO of the case stated that the scooter was seized from the house of injured Tushar Ahuja.

PW Ct Ravinder stated that after he went to PS for registration of FIR, IO/SI Rajesh Kumar along with complainant and accused came to PS and they went to the spot where site plan Ex. PW3/B was prepared whereas PW Rajesh Kumar stated that only he along with complainant/Tushar went to the spot.
PW Raj Kumar stated in his testimony that the accident happened at G Block, Sector 15, Rohini whereas PW Puneet stated that the spot of accident was infront of gate of EBlock, Sector 15, Rohini.
Thus, the testimonies of PWs are at variance with each other.

21. The most important fact in the present case is that PW Dr. Deepti Bhalla stated that when injured/PW Puneet was brought to BSA hospital for medical examination, smell of alcohol was present in his breath.
It is pertinent to mention that injured/PW Puneet was the driver of the scooter against which the offending vehicle had collided.
This fact has neither been mentioned in the charge sheet nor has the same been explained by the prosecution.
The PW SI Rajesh Kumar stated in his cross examination that he did not know about the fact that at the time of accident, injured/PW Puneet was under the influence of alcohol.
PW Gurjant Singh who was the second IO of the case also stated that he was not aware about the fact that injured persons were in under the influence of alcohol.

22. The prosecution examined two public witness who were present near to the spot of accident i.e PW Raj Kumar and PW/injured Puneet; PW Tushar could not be examined since he expired during the pendency of the trial.
From the testimony of PW Raj Kumar it is clear that he did not witness the accident himself as came to the spot only when he heard the noise.
The only eye witness left is PW/injured Puneet.
PW Puneet stated in his testimony that accused was driving his vehicle in high speed and in zig zag manner.
PW Puneet has not been cross examined by the accused.
However, as mentioned above, PW Dr. Deepti who medically examined PW/injured Puneet at BSA hospital found alcohol in his breath.
Thus, this Court has to be circumspect in accepting the testimony of PW Puneet and must look for corroboration by other evidence.
There are no other independent witnesses who witnessed the incident.
It is already observed above that the testimonies of PW Raj Kumar, PW Ct Ravinder, PW Puneet and PW Rajesh Kumar are at variance with each other.

In the absence of any other witness or evidence, it would be difficult to accept that the accident was caused due to rashness or negligence on the part of accused in driving the vehicle since as per MLC the injured Puneet himself was under the influence of alcohol.

23. In view of the above said discussion, it is clear that prosecution has not been able to prove that the offending vehicle was driven by the accused in rash or negligent manner and that the injuries to Tushar Ahuja and Puneet were caused due to rashness or negligence on the part of the accused while driving the offending vehicle.

Thus, the prosecution has failed to prove its case against the accused State vs . Mukul Singh on 9 March, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/12061482/
9
Mukul Singh for offences punishable under section 279/337/338 IPC.
Accordingly, accused Mukul Singh is acquitted of the charges under section 279/337/338 IPC.

opennyai_summary.ANALYSIS:
16. In a criminal trial, the onus remains on the prosecution to prove the guilt of accused beyond all reasonable doubts and benefit of doubt, if any, must necessarily go in favour of the accused.
It is for the prosecution to travel the entire distance from may have to must have.
If the prosecution appears to be improbable or lacks credibility the benefit of doubt necessarily has to go to the accused.
Observations in a recent decision of this Court, Shivaji Sahabrao Bobade & Anr.
v. State of Maharashtra (1973 2 SCC 793) to which reference has been made during arguments were not intended to make a departure from the rule of the presumption of innocence of the accused and his entitlement to the benefit of reasonable doubt in criminal cases.
One of the cardinal principles which has always to be kept in view in our system of administration of justice for criminal cases is that a person arraigned as an accused is presumed to be innocent unless that presumption is rebutted by the prosecution by production of evidence as may show him to be guilty of the offence with which he is charged.
The burden of proving the guilt of the accused is upon the prosecution and unless it relieves itself of that burden, the courts cannot record a finding of the guilt of the accused.
There are certain cases in which statutory presumptions arise regarding the guilt of the accused, but the burden even in those cases is upon the prosecution to prove the existence of facts which have to be present before the presumption can be drawn.
Once those facts are shown by the prosecution to exist, the court can raise the statutory presumption and it would, in such an event,
be for the accused to rebut the presumption.
The onus even in such cases upon the accused is not as heavy as is normally upon the prosecution to prove the guilt of the accused.
If some material is brought on the record consistent with the innocence of the accused which may reasonably be true, even though it is not positively proved to be true, the accused would be entitled to acquittal.
This principle has a special relevance in cases wherein the guilt of the accused is sought to be established by circumstantial evidence.
When they were in front of gate of EBlock, Sector 15, Rohini, the accused who was driving the offending vehicle bearing registration No. DL 8SCM 2612 TATA Indica car hit the scooter driven by the injured Puneet and Tushar from right side while turning his car to EBlock due to which injured Puneet received grievous injury and Tushar received simple injury.
The accused was charged with offences punishable u/s 279/337/338 IPC.
That Sh. Puneet received grievous injury and Sh. Tushar Ahuja received simple injury.
ii. That the injuries received by the injured persons due to the accident caused by the offending vehicle which was driven by the accused.
It is therefore, sufficiently proved that the injured Puneet received grievous injury and Tushar Ahuja received simple injury which was due to road accident.
He admitted that he was being served with notice u/s 133 M.V Act Ex.
PW2/A to which he replied with Ex. PW2/A.
The accused did not dispute the mechanical inspection report Ex. A19 (colly).
The offending vehicle was found to be having damage on the right side of the body while the scooter of the injured persons was also found to be having damage on right side of the body.
Therefore, this Court is of the considered opinion that there is no dispute regarding the identity of the accused as well as offending vehicle.
20. Now, the most essential ingredient to be proved by the prosecution for securing the conviction for the charge under section 279/337/338 IPC is that the injuries suffered by the injured persons is the direct result of the rash or negligent driving by the accused.
PW Puneet has not been cross examined by the accused.
However, as mentioned above, PW Dr. Deepti who medically examined PW/injured Puneet at BSA hospital found alcohol in his breath.
Thus, this Court has to be circumspect in accepting the testimony of PW Puneet and must look for corroboration by other evidence.
There are no other independent witnesses who witnessed the incident.
It is already observed above that the testimonies of PW Raj Kumar, PW Ct Ravinder, PW Puneet and PW Rajesh Kumar are at variance with each other.
In the absence of any other witness or evidence, it would be difficult to accept that the accident was caused due to rashness or negligence on the part of accused in driving the vehicle since as per MLC the injured Puneet himself was under the influence of alcohol.
23. In view of the above said discussion, it is clear that prosecution has not been able to prove that the offending vehicle was driven by the accused in rash or negligent manner and that the injuries to Tushar Ahuja and Puneet were caused due to rashness or negligence on the part of the accused while driving the offending vehicle.
